name: Nguồn
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Nguyễn Phú Phong. 1996. The Nguồn language of Quảng Bình, Vietnam. Mon-Khmer Studies 26:179-190. (open scan:http://sealang.net/archives/mks/pdf/26:scanned copy)
catalog_quote: In Nguồn, as in Vietnamese, words are largely monosyllabic. Each syllable contains an initial, a nucleus and a tone. We examine successively these elements in comparison with Vietnamese whose phonetic system is well known. [...] [3.4 Tones, p.187] The description of the tone system uses the etymological notation with numbers. Therefore, tones are distributed into two series, high (first register) and low (second register). [...] Those six tones are distributed into three categories: A (1, 2), B (3, 4) and C (5, 6). To the extent that syllables ending in a stop form a separate category labeled D, Nguồn and Vietnamese alike will have an 8-tone system: the two extra tones are: (ap7/áp) and (ap8/ạp). Phonetic features of Nguồn tones are not the same as Vietnamese. [...] [p.188] Tone 3 is a rising tone; tone 4 is a falling one; both are glottalized at the end. Because of the intonation contours of 4 and 6, these two tones are often hard to distinguish.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: is a real 12-page scan-only PDF (no text) of Nguyen Phu Phong 1996, MKS 26:179-190, downloaded from the open SEAlang MKS archive (URL); scanned in and scanned/. I read the page scan directly (p.2 = journal p.180, p.9 = p.187). Both quoted passages are there verbatim: p.180 sec. 3 'Phonology': 'In Nguồn, as in Vietnamese, words are largely monosyllabic. Each syllable contains an initial, a nucleus and a tone. We examine successively these elements in comparison with Vietnamese whose phonetic system is well known.'; p.187 sec. 3.4 'Tones': '..Those six tones are distributed into three categories: A (1, 2), B (3, 4) and C (5, 6). To the extent that syllables ending in a stop form a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nguồn is described as a monosyllabic lexical-tone language of the Vietnamese/Mường type (6 tones on sonorant-final syllables + 2 on checked syllables; 5 tones in Ferlus's Bốc Thọ data); the source assigns every syllable a tone and says nothing about word stress, so no stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Dialect differences (Cổ Liêm vs Yên Thọ) concern segments and tone realisation; tones 4 and 6 often hard to distinguish; speakers sometimes substitute Vietnamese tones.
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable = word for most of the lexicon (monosyllabic); description based on elicited citation forms from two dialects (Cổ Liêm, Yên Thọ/An Thọ, Minh Hoá district). No statement about prominence in the few polysyllables/compounds.
new_statements.identity_note: Phong 1996 describes two Nguồn dialects, Cổ Liêm (Trung Hoá commune) and Yên Thọ/An Thọ (Tân Hoá), Minh Hoá district, Quảng Bình = Glottolog nguo1239 (no sub-dialect codes). Ferlus 1998's tone data are from Bốc Thọ (= Yên Thọ). Some Vietnamese authors (Nguyễn Văn Tài) treat Nguồn as a Mường dialect; the language-level match to nguo1239 is not in doubt.

new_statements.quote: enfin tous sont prononcés, quant à l'accent (1), d'une manière autre que dans le bas Sông-Gianh. [n.1:] Je suis obligé de laisser de côté la question de l'accent. Les accents sont prononcés d'une manière toute différente des accents du bas Sông-Gianh. Quelques accents s'assimilent-ils, ou se dédoublent-ils, c'est-à-dire combien y a-t-il d'accents dans la langue, je n'ai pu m'en rendre compte. Je noterai donc les mots avec l'accent qu'ils ont ordinairement en annamite. Il faut remarquer que les Nguồn démarquent les accents. [...] (ce disant, il prononçait l'accent hỏi à sa manière).
new_statements.translation: finally all [the words] are pronounced, as regards the accent [= tone] (1), in a manner different from that of the lower Sông-Gianh. [n.1:] I am obliged to set aside the question of the accent [tone]. The accents are pronounced in a manner entirely different from the accents of the lower Sông-Gianh. Whether some accents merge, or split, that is, how many accents there are in the language, I have not been able to determine. I shall therefore note the words with the accent they ordinarily have in Vietnamese. It should be noted that the Nguồn distinguish the accents. [...] (saying this, he pronounced the hỏi accent in his own way).

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing Phong 1996 statement: Nguồn is tonal, no word-stress statement. Adds only that the tones differ markedly from lowland Vietnamese and were not counted. The catalog record itself has an empty rule, and nothing here supplies a stress placement. Read from Gallica's BEFEO tome V scan (ark:/12148/bpt6k93380v, f357-f375 = pp.349-367) after the Persée docAsPDF could not be reached by automated download altcha twice; several Gallica JPEGs arrived truncated (server throttling within --max-time 120) and were re-rendered via PIL or re-downloaded at width 2000 (f370); key passages transcribed by eye from the page scan because the scanned garbled the footnote.
new_statements.rule_in_words: 'Accent' in Cadière's 1905 usage is the Vietnamese lexical tone ('l'accent hỏi' = the hỏi tone, illustrated with biển 'sea'). He states that Nguồn has tones, that they are realised quite differently from those of lowland Quảng Bình Vietnamese, that he could not determine their number (whether some merge or split), and that he therefore writes each word with its ordinary Vietnamese tone. Nothing is said about word stress or prominence; Nguồn words are treated as monosyllables throughout.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone inventory explicitly left undetermined (n.1, p.356). Separate statement on p.362 that the Sách language 'a des accents' (pli 'fruit' high/head voice vs pli 'drunk' lower; presyllables pe, ke, me lower than the following syllable) concerns Sách, not Nguồn.
new_statements.identity_note: Cadière 1905 describes the Nguồn (self-name; Sino-Vietnamese Nam-Nguyên) of the middle Nguồn-Nậy and upper Nguồn-Nan valleys of the Sông-Gianh, northern Quảng Bình, from a 1900 visit; his p.362 tone remarks concern the neighbouring Sách (Thất-Sách, a Chứt variety), a different language. Chéon 1907 works only from Cadière's Nguồn and Sách word lists, comparing them with Mường of the Black River and Vietnamese.
